appraisal_events.evidence: je l'ai trouvé curieux. Je ne l'ai pas trouvé simple !... comme un œillet vert, c'est-à-dire une chose qui m'étonne et ne me plaît pas infiniment... qu'on aurait fait aussi bien de ne pas pouvoir
appraisal_events.explanation: The princesse offers a backhanded, socially coded critique of Elstir (implicitly the subject of the prior exchange), calling his work a curious, artificial 'obtenu' effect that does not really please her, a mixed but net-unflattering local judgment.

appraisal_events.evidence: il a sur les œuvres d'art un goût en quelque sorte infaillible, il ne se trompe jamais ; si quelque chose est beau, il le reconnaît tout de suite, il le prend en haine... S'il pleure, on achète la pièce... Si ses yeux restent secs, on la renvoie au marchand et on le poursuit pour faux.
appraisal_events.explanation: Under the guise of praising the emperor's infallible taste, the prince's account systematically shows his judgment to be exactly inverted (he hates what is good, likes what is fake), an ironic diminishment confirmed socially when everyone smiles at the joke.

status_effects.explanation: The emperor's taste and judgment are locally discredited by the prince's ironic anecdote, which the assembled company recognizes and smiles at.
The prince's elaborate, well-received ironic performance (met with smiles from the whole table) gives him local rhetorical standing as a witty raconteur.
The princesse's ambivalent, faintly dismissive assessment of his work as contrived and not truly pleasing somewhat lowers Elstir's local standing in this exchange.

ambiguities: The pronoun 'lui'/'il' that the princesse discusses is resolved to Elstir only via the immediately preceding turn (the prince's remark about M. Elstir); Elstir is never named within the passage itself.
'l'empereur' is not on the reference sheet and is not otherwise named in the passage; it is left as an unresolved surface form rather than identified with a specific historical figure.
